script.opening: "Hi, I'm ringing about my blood result — the receptionist said my red cells are 'large' or something? I immediately panicked and googled it and now I'm terrified it's leukaemia or something with my blood. I feel mostly okay, just tired. What does it mean that my cells are big? Should I be worried?"

facts.text: If asked: tired for about four months, sleeping badly.
No bruising, no nosebleeds, no infections, no night sweats, no weight loss, no lumps. No pins and needles or numbness. No sore tongue. Bowels normal. Periods regular, not heavy.
You eat meat and vegetables, "not as well as I should lately". No regular medicines, no supplements, no allergies.
No feeling cold, no weight gain, no dry skin that you have noticed.

facts.topic: Alcohol — only if asked in an open, non-judgemental way
facts.text: At first: "Just a glass of wine in the evening." If the doctor asks gently about how much exactly, or says many people drink more when going through a hard time: "Honestly... it's a bottle most nights now. Sometimes a bit more at weekends." It has crept up over about six months. No morning drinking, no shakes. You know it is too much.

facts.topic: What happened six months ago — only if asked what changed
facts.text: Your mum died suddenly in the spring, and two months later your husband moved out. "I just sit on my own in the evenings and the wine helps me not think."
Low, tearful, not enjoying much. Still working (receptionist at a dental practice). No thoughts of harming yourself. Your sister lives nearby and calls often.
46, two teenage sons who live with you half the week. Non-smoker. Drives.

Very anxious about leukaemia at first. Once the doctor explains that large red cells on their own are usually not a blood cancer and have common causes, you calm down. If alcohol is asked about in a judgemental way, under-report and become defensive. If asked kindly, tell the truth with some shame and become tearful talking about your mum. Respond well to support and a plan.

ice.ideas: "Big cells means something wrong with my blood — maybe leukaemia."
ice.concerns: Leukaemia. Underneath (only if trust is built): your drinking and how alone you feel since Mum died and your husband left.
ice.expectations: "Should I be worried?" You want to know what happens next. You would welcome help once you feel safe to talk.

cues: "I'm terrified it's leukaemia." — say in the opening.
"I've not been sleeping well since... well, it's been a hard year." — say if asked about tiredness.
"The wine helps me not think." — say only if alcohol has been raised kindly.

checkpoints.text: Reassures accurately that isolated MACROCYTOSIS (raised MCV without anaemia, normal WCC/platelets) is usually NOT sinister and leukaemia is not the typical cause — it is a finding to work up, not a diagnosis — without dismissing it

Plans a STRUCTURED cause work-up: B12 and folate, TFTs, LFTs (including GGT), reticulocytes/blood film, and a medication review — covering the common causes (alcohol, B12/folate, hypothyroidism, drugs, liver disease)
Takes a NON-JUDGEMENTAL ALCOHOL history that creates space for honest disclosure (recognising alcohol as a very common cause of macrocytosis), and so uncovers the rising intake

Recognises and addresses the underlying DISTRESS: the recent bereavement/relationship stress driving the drinking — screening mood and offering support — treating the result as a door to a sensitive, important issue rather than just a number

Knows when to escalate/refer: unexplained macrocytosis, associated cytopenias, abnormal film, or progression warrant haematology/marrow consideration — distinguishing this from her likely benign, identifiable cause
Reassures about the leukaemia fear genuinely, then gently opens the alcohol/lifestyle door without judgement, so she feels safe to disclose rather than shamed into hiding
Responds with compassion to the bereavement/distress, framing the result as an opportunity for help, and engages her in addressing both the drinking and the grief

Safety-nets and follows up: the cause work-up (B12/folate/TFTs/LFTs/film), alcohol-reduction support and mood support/bereavement help, recheck of the FBC/MCV, escalation criteria if unexplained, and a follow-up that treats the person, not just the result

worked.txt: "Let me take the scariest thought off the table first: large red cells, especially with the rest of your blood count completely normal and no anaemia, is almost never leukaemia. So please breathe. It’s a finding we look into, not a diagnosis — and the common causes are all pretty ordinary and fixable."

"The usual reasons red cells run a bit large are things like low vitamin B12 or folate, an underactive thyroid, certain medications, the liver, or alcohol. So rather than worry, we just check through those with a few blood tests and sort whatever we find."

"Can I ask a few honest questions, no judgement at all — it just helps me find the cause? How are things with alcohol at the moment — has it crept up recently? … Thank you for being straight with me. That’s really useful, and it’s likely the explanation for the result — which is good, because it’s very fixable."

"It sounds like the drinking has gone up since you lost… … I’m so sorry. That makes complete sense — a lot of people lean on a drink to get through grief, and it’s nothing to be ashamed of. But your body’s quietly showing the effect, which is actually a helpful early nudge. How have you been in yourself, with the grief and everything?"

"So this blood test, weirdly, might be a useful thing — it’s flagged the drinking before it’s caused harm, and it lets me help you with both the alcohol and how you’re coping. We can cut the drinking back with support, and get you some help with the grief if you’d like. The blood usually settles once the alcohol eases."

"I’ll do the full set of tests — B12, folate, thyroid, liver — to be thorough, and we’ll recheck the count. If anything were unexplained or other parts of the blood changed, I’d involve a specialist — but I don’t expect that. Let’s book a proper follow-up for the drinking and the grief. You rang terrified of leukaemia; what this really is, is a chance to look after you."

f.learning: Isolated macrocytosis (raised MCV without anaemia, normal white cells/platelets) is usually NOT sinister — leukaemia is not the typical cause — and is a finding to work up through its common causes: ALCOHOL (very common), B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, drugs, and liver disease, with a structured panel (B12, folate, TFTs, LFTs/GGT, reticulocytes/film, medication review) and haematology/marrow referral reserved for unexplained, progressive or multi-lineage abnormalities. The examinable hidden agenda is that the likely cause — rising alcohol since a recent bereavement/relationship stress — is something the patient is ashamed of and has framed the call around a leukaemia fear partly to avoid; the result is a DOOR into a sensitive, important issue. Reassure genuinely about leukaemia, take a non-judgemental alcohol/lifestyle history that enables disclosure, and address the underlying distress (screen mood, offer bereavement and alcohol-reduction support) — treating the abnormal result as an opportunity to help, not just a number to recheck. Catching rising alcohol early (the macrocytosis is a useful biological flag) and addressing the bereavement/low mood is genuinely valuable — the abnormal result is an opportunity, not just a number to recheck. Done well, it opens help she might not otherwise have sought.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · NICE NG145 (thyroid disease, 2019) · NICE PH24 (alcohol-use disorders: prevention, 2010) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders: dependence, 2011) · NICE CG100 (alcohol-use disorders: physical complications, 2010) · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
knowledge.summary: An MCV of 105 with a normal haemoglobin, white count and platelets is a finding to explain, not a sign of leukaemia. Work up the common causes, take a non-judgemental alcohol history, and respond to the grief behind the drinking.

points.t: A raised MCV with normal haemoglobin, white cells and platelets usually has a benign, identifiable cause. Leukaemia typically presents with other abnormal counts or symptoms, not an isolated MCV rise.

Alcohol, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs (for example methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide, some anticonvulsants and antiretrovirals), reticulocytosis after bleeding or haemolysis, and pregnancy. Primary marrow disorders such as myelodysplasia are less common.

B12 and folate (NICE NG239 covers B12 testing and treatment), TSH (NICE NG145), liver tests including GGT, reticulocyte count and a blood film, with a medication review and an honest alcohol history. Repeat the FBC after addressing the cause; red cells live about 120 days, so the MCV takes a few months to settle.
Unexplained macrocytosis after the work-up, falling haemoglobin or other cytopenias, an abnormal film such as dysplastic features, or a progressive rise warrant haematology advice.

NICE PH24: use AUDIT-C, then the full AUDIT if positive, and give structured brief advice. UK CMO: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days. Assess for dependence and withdrawal risk (NICE CG115); if dependent, advise not to stop suddenly and arrange assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115).

Rising drinking after a bereavement or relationship stress often signals distress. Screen mood and suicide risk. NICE NG222: offer treatment matched to severity and preference; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral; bereavement support services help with grief itself.

dg.d: Confirmed identity, invited her fear, and reassured early and honestly about leukaemia.
Bereavement, difficulties at home, support around her and how she has been coping.
B12, folate, TSH, liver tests including GGT, reticulocytes, blood film; repeat FBC in a few months.
Alcohol versus B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs and marrow disorders.
Screened for bleeding, bruising, infection, sweats and weight loss; asked about suicide risk and alcohol withdrawal.
Isolated macrocytosis most likely from increased alcohol, linked to grief and low mood.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: AUDIT-C and brief advice (NICE PH24); a goal she chose; withdrawal safety advice (NICE CG100).
Low mood screened; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral and bereavement support offered (NICE NG222).
Results call, review in about four weeks, haematology if unexplained or other counts fall, same-day contact for worsening mood.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the pause and “more than I used to”, and explored the driver behind the drinking.
Idea (leukaemia), concern (serious blood disease; unspoken shame about drinking), expectation (to know what “big cells” means).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Leukaemia. Underneath (only if trust is built): your drinking and how alone you feel since Mum died and your husband left — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Brennan? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just confirm your date of birth? … Thank you. I understand you’ve been worried since hearing about your result — what’s been going through your mind?
model.why: Confirms identity on the phone and opens with her concern

model.text: I panicked. The receptionist said my red cells are large, and I googled it and now I’m terrified it’s leukaemia. I feel mostly okay, just tired. Should I be worried?

I’m sorry you’ve had that worry hanging over you. Let me take the biggest fear off the table straight away: large red cells, with the rest of your blood count completely normal, is very rarely anything to do with leukaemia. Can I explain what it usually means, ask you a few questions, and then agree a plan?
model.why: Gives honest, early reassurance about the specific fear before exploring

model.text: Yes. Okay. That’s a relief already.

So, your red cells are a little larger than average. Your haemoglobin, white cells and platelets are all normal. That pattern usually has an everyday cause, and my job is to find which one. Tell me about the tiredness — how long, and what’s it like?
model.why: Explains the result simply and moves to open data gathering

model.text: A while now. Just flat, I suppose.
Any breathlessness, bruising, bleeding, infections, night sweats or weight loss?
model.why: Screens for features that would point to a marrow problem

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Any tingling in your hands or feet, a sore tongue, or feeling the cold or putting on weight?
model.why: Screens for B12 deficiency and hypothyroidism

model.text: Not really.
Are you taking any medicines, supplements or anything from the chemist?
No, nothing regular.

One of the commonest causes of larger red cells is alcohol, so I ask everyone about it — no judgement at all, it just helps me find the answer. How much would you say you drink in a typical week at the moment?
model.why: Normalises and asks a non-judgemental alcohol question

model.text: … More than I used to. Quite a lot more, if I’m honest.
Thank you for being straight with me — that genuinely helps. Has something changed that led to that?
model.why: Acknowledges disclosure and gently explores the driver

model.text: It’s been a hard time. There was a bereavement, and things at home have been difficult. A drink in the evening helped me switch off. Then it just crept up.
I’m so sorry. That’s a lot to carry. Many people lean on a drink to get through grief — it’s nothing to be ashamed of. How have you been in yourself, in your mood?
model.why: Responds with compassion and moves to mood

model.text: Low, if I’m honest.
Thank you for telling me. Can I ask — have you had any thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or of harming yourself?
model.why: Asks directly about risk with alcohol and low mood

model.text: No. Nothing like that. I’ve just been getting through.
I’m glad. If that ever changed, I’d want you to tell us straight away. Would it help to go through a few quick questions about the drinking, so we can see where things are?
model.why: Moves to structured AUDIT-C screening with consent

model.text: Okay.

How often do you have a drink, how many on a typical day, and how often six or more in one go? … Thank you. From what you’ve said, you’re drinking above the low-risk guideline of 14 units a week. Do you ever feel shaky, sweaty or unwell in the morning until you have a drink?
model.why: Quantifies with AUDIT-C and screens for dependence and withdrawal

model.text: I don’t think so. I’d have to think about it.

That’s fine. Here’s how I see it. The most likely reason for your larger red cells is the extra alcohol, and the good news is that it usually settles once the drinking comes down. But I want to be thorough, so I’ll also check B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests, look at your cells under the microscope, and recheck the count in a few months.
model.why: Gives the working diagnosis and a structured work-up

model.text: So it’s not my blood — it’s me drinking.
It’s your body giving you an early nudge, before any harm is done. That’s actually helpful. It gives us a chance to look after you — the drinking and the grief behind it.
model.why: Reframes the result as an opportunity, not a verdict

model.text: I suppose it is. I didn’t want to face it.
What would feel realistic for you to start with — cutting down, having some drink-free days, something else?
Maybe no drinking on weeknights to start with.

That’s a great first goal. One important safety point: if you do notice shakes, sweats or feeling very unwell when you cut down, don’t stop suddenly — ring us, as that needs support. I can also give you details for local alcohol support, bereavement support, and NHS Talking Therapies, which you can refer yourself to. Which would you like?
model.why: Brief intervention with withdrawal safety and support options (NICE PH24, CG100)

model.text: Maybe the bereavement support. And the talking therapy.
I’ll send both by text. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
Bloods for B12 and thyroid and liver, no drinking on weeknights, the bereavement and talking therapy numbers, and ring if I get shaky.

Perfect. I’ll ring you with the results, and I’d like to speak again in about four weeks to see how you’re getting on. If your mood drops or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. You rang terrified of leukaemia — what this really is, is a chance to look after you.
model.why: Defined follow-up, mood safety-net and a compassionate close

model.text: Thank you, doctor. I actually feel lighter.

social.t: Bereavement and relationship strain commonly drive increased drinking. Shame keeps it hidden; a normalising approach helps disclosure.
Ask who she can talk to; grief and drinking often isolate people. Offer community bereavement services.

legal.t: Nothing to notify today. If alcohol misuse or dependence is later diagnosed, the DVLA requires notification — explain this honestly if it arises.

professional.t: Confirm identity before discussing results. Sensitive disclosures by phone need extra checking of understanding and a clear follow-up plan.
Reception staff relaying partial results (“large cells”) caused avoidable anxiety. Consider practice feedback on how abnormal results are communicated.

community.t: Local community alcohol services; Drinkline; Cruse Bereavement Support; NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); Samaritans for crisis support.

redFlags: Bleeding, bruising, recurrent infection, night sweats or weight loss — possible marrow disorder
Other abnormal counts or an abnormal blood film — haematology advice
Neurological symptoms such as numbness or unsteadiness — possible B12 deficiency
Suicidal thoughts, or morning shakes and sweats suggesting alcohol dependence
psychosocial: Alcohol pattern, asked in a normalised way, with AUDIT-C
Bereavement, home stress and who she has to talk to
ice: Concern: a serious blood disease; unspoken shame about the drinking
Expectation: to understand the result and hear it isn’t leukaemia

playbook.diagnosis: Isolated macrocytosis most likely related to increased alcohol intake, in the context of bereavement and low mood, with other causes to exclude: “Your red cells are slightly large, most likely from the extra alcohol, and it usually settles when drinking comes down.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your red cells as a quiet record of the last few months. They’ve noticed the extra drinking before anything else has — an early warning, not a disease.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang terrified this was leukaemia. It isn’t pointing that way — and the thing it is pointing to is something we can help with.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the grief as the driver; offer bereavement support and NHS Talking Therapies alongside alcohol reduction, and agree a goal she chose.
sharedPlan: B12, folate, TSH, liver tests including GGT, reticulocytes and a blood film; repeat FBC in a few months
AUDIT-C and brief advice (NICE PH24); weeknight drink-free goal; withdrawal safety advice (NICE CG100)
Mood support: Talking Therapies self-referral and bereavement support (NICE NG222)
safetyNet: Shakes or sweats when cutting down: don’t stop suddenly, contact the practice
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm: same-day contact or NHS 111 mental health option; review in about four weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is about the person behind an unremarkable number. It is failed by filing the result with a recheck, by alarming the patient, or by an alcohol question that shuts disclosure down.

items.fail: “It’s only slightly raised — we’ll repeat it in three months.”
items.why: Macrocytosis is a finding to explain. Rechecking without a work-up misses B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease and the alcohol.
items.fix: Arrange B12, folate, TSH, liver tests, reticulocytes and a film, and take an alcohol history.

items.fail: Listing leukaemia among possible causes to be thorough.
items.why: She rang frightened of exactly that. Unbalanced lists increase anxiety and reduce trust.
items.fix: Reassure honestly first: “With the rest of your count normal, this is very rarely leukaemia.”

items.fail: Asking “Do you drink too much?” and accepting “no, not really”.
items.why: A loaded question invites denial and misses the most likely cause and the grief behind it.
items.fix: Normalise: “Alcohol is a common cause, so I ask everyone — no judgement.” Then pause and let her answer.

items.fail: Advising her to stop drinking completely from tonight.
items.why: If she is dependent, abrupt cessation risks withdrawal. NICE CG100 covers assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: Screen for morning shakes and sweats; agree a gradual goal; “If you get shaky when cutting down, ring us — don’t stop suddenly.”

items.fail: Treating the drinking without asking about mood or suicide risk.
items.why: Grief, low mood and alcohol together raise risk; missing this is a serious omission.
items.fix: “How have you been in yourself?” then ask directly about thoughts of self-harm.

items.fail: Ending the phone call without confirming the plan or a follow-up.
items.why: Telephone consultations need explicit checks; no follow-up is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back, a results call, and a review in about four weeks.

timeMap.d: Confirm identity. She opens terrified of leukaemia — address it honestly within the first minute.
Tiredness, marrow red flags, B12 and thyroid symptoms, medicines. Then a normalised alcohol question and the pause that follows.
Bereavement, home stress, low mood. Ask about suicide risk; AUDIT-C and withdrawal screen.
Likely alcohol-related macrocytosis; full work-up; a goal she chooses; withdrawal safety; bereavement and Talking Therapies.
Results call, review in about four weeks, same-day contact if mood worsens.

wordPics.fail: Says “it’s probably nothing, we’ll recheck in three months”; or lists leukaemia among the causes; never asks about alcohol, or asks in a judgemental way; misses the bereavement and low mood.
wordPics.pass: Reassures accurately, arranges B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests, takes an alcohol history that uncovers the increase, and offers support with follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: normalises the alcohol question so disclosure feels safe, responds warmly to the grief, screens mood and suicide risk, uses AUDIT-C and withdrawal advice, lets her choose her goal, and frames the result as an opportunity.

avoid.dont: “Causes include alcohol, vitamin deficiency and, rarely, leukaemia or bone marrow problems.”
avoid.instead: “With the rest of your count normal, this is very rarely anything to do with leukaemia.”
avoid.why: Listing her worst fear as a possibility amplifies anxiety she rang with.

avoid.instead: “Alcohol is a common cause, so I ask everyone — no judgement. How much do you drink in a typical week at the moment?”
avoid.why: A loaded question invites denial; a normalised one invites honesty.

avoid.dont: “Just cut down the drinking and we’ll recheck the blood.”
avoid.instead: “It sounds like the drinking went up after a really hard time. How have you been in yourself?”
avoid.why: Treating the number without the grief misses the real consultation.

It’s your body giving you an early nudge, before any harm is done. That’s actually helpful. It gives us a chance to look after you — the drinking and the grief behind it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes the result as an opportunity, not a verdict

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose it is. I didn’t want to face it.
What would feel realistic for you to start with — cutting down, having some drink-free days, something else?
Maybe no drinking on weeknights to start with.

That’s a great first goal. One important safety point: if you do notice shakes, sweats or feeling very unwell when you cut down, don’t stop suddenly — ring us, as that needs support. I can also give you details for local alcohol support, bereavement support, and NHS Talking Therapies, which you can refer yourself to. Which would you like?
SCA_MODELS.why: Brief intervention with withdrawal safety and support options (NICE PH24, CG100)

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe the bereavement support. And the talking therapy.
I’ll send both by text. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
Bloods for B12 and thyroid and liver, no drinking on weeknights, the bereavement and talking therapy numbers, and ring if I get shaky.

Perfect. I’ll ring you with the results, and I’d like to speak again in about four weeks to see how you’re getting on. If your mood drops or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. You rang terrified of leukaemia — what this really is, is a chance to look after you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined follow-up, mood safety-net and a compassionate close

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. I actually feel lighter.

SCA_STEM.name: Lisa Brennan
pmh: None recorded relevant to this result
SCA_STEM.recent: FBC for tiredness: MCV 105 fL; haemoglobin, white cells and platelets normal. B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests not yet requested.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call for her blood result. Told by reception her red cells are “large”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · NICE NG145 (thyroid disease, 2019) · NICE PH24 (alcohol-use disorders: prevention, 2010) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders: dependence, 2011) · NICE CG100 (alcohol-use disorders: physical complications, 2010) · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An MCV of 105 with a normal haemoglobin, white count and platelets is a finding to explain, not a sign of leukaemia. Work up the common causes, take a non-judgemental alcohol history, and respond to the grief behind the drinking.

points.t: A raised MCV with normal haemoglobin, white cells and platelets usually has a benign, identifiable cause. Leukaemia typically presents with other abnormal counts or symptoms, not an isolated MCV rise.

Alcohol, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs (for example methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide, some anticonvulsants and antiretrovirals), reticulocytosis after bleeding or haemolysis, and pregnancy. Primary marrow disorders such as myelodysplasia are less common.

B12 and folate (NICE NG239 covers B12 testing and treatment), TSH (NICE NG145), liver tests including GGT, reticulocyte count and a blood film, with a medication review and an honest alcohol history. Repeat the FBC after addressing the cause; red cells live about 120 days, so the MCV takes a few months to settle.
Unexplained macrocytosis after the work-up, falling haemoglobin or other cytopenias, an abnormal film such as dysplastic features, or a progressive rise warrant haematology advice.

NICE PH24: use AUDIT-C, then the full AUDIT if positive, and give structured brief advice. UK CMO: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days. Assess for dependence and withdrawal risk (NICE CG115); if dependent, advise not to stop suddenly and arrange assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115).

Rising drinking after a bereavement or relationship stress often signals distress. Screen mood and suicide risk. NICE NG222: offer treatment matched to severity and preference; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral; bereavement support services help with grief itself.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity, invited her fear, and reassured early and honestly about leukaemia.
Bereavement, difficulties at home, support around her and how she has been coping.
Picked up the pause and “more than I used to”, and explored the driver behind the drinking.
Idea (leukaemia), concern (serious blood disease; unspoken shame about drinking), expectation (to know what “big cells” means).
B12, folate, TSH, liver tests including GGT, reticulocytes, blood film; repeat FBC in a few months.
Alcohol versus B12 or folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs and marrow disorders.
Screened for bleeding, bruising, infection, sweats and weight loss; asked about suicide risk and alcohol withdrawal.
Isolated macrocytosis most likely from increased alcohol, linked to grief and low mood.
AUDIT-C and brief advice (NICE PH24); a goal she chose; withdrawal safety advice (NICE CG100).
Low mood screened; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral and bereavement support offered (NICE NG222).
Results call, review in about four weeks, haematology if unexplained or other counts fall, same-day contact for worsening mood.

social.t: Bereavement and relationship strain commonly drive increased drinking. Shame keeps it hidden; a normalising approach helps disclosure.
Ask who she can talk to; grief and drinking often isolate people. Offer community bereavement services.

legal.t: Nothing to notify today. If alcohol misuse or dependence is later diagnosed, the DVLA requires notification — explain this honestly if it arises.

professional.t: Confirm identity before discussing results. Sensitive disclosures by phone need extra checking of understanding and a clear follow-up plan.
Reception staff relaying partial results (“large cells”) caused avoidable anxiety. Consider practice feedback on how abnormal results are communicated.

community.t: Local community alcohol services; Drinkline; Cruse Bereavement Support; NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); Samaritans for crisis support.

redFlags: Bleeding, bruising, recurrent infection, night sweats or weight loss — possible marrow disorder
Other abnormal counts or an abnormal blood film — haematology advice
Neurological symptoms such as numbness or unsteadiness — possible B12 deficiency
Suicidal thoughts, or morning shakes and sweats suggesting alcohol dependence
psychosocial: Alcohol pattern, asked in a normalised way, with AUDIT-C
Bereavement, home stress and who she has to talk to
ice: Concern: a serious blood disease; unspoken shame about the drinking
Expectation: to understand the result and hear it isn’t leukaemia

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Isolated macrocytosis most likely related to increased alcohol intake, in the context of bereavement and low mood, with other causes to exclude: “Your red cells are slightly large, most likely from the extra alcohol, and it usually settles when drinking comes down.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your red cells as a quiet record of the last few months. They’ve noticed the extra drinking before anything else has — an early warning, not a disease.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang terrified this was leukaemia. It isn’t pointing that way — and the thing it is pointing to is something we can help with.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the grief as the driver; offer bereavement support and NHS Talking Therapies alongside alcohol reduction, and agree a goal she chose.
sharedPlan: B12, folate, TSH, liver tests including GGT, reticulocytes and a blood film; repeat FBC in a few months
AUDIT-C and brief advice (NICE PH24); weeknight drink-free goal; withdrawal safety advice (NICE CG100)
Mood support: Talking Therapies self-referral and bereavement support (NICE NG222)
safetyNet: Shakes or sweats when cutting down: don’t stop suddenly, contact the practice
Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm: same-day contact or NHS 111 mental health option; review in about four weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about the person behind an unremarkable number. It is failed by filing the result with a recheck, by alarming the patient, or by an alcohol question that shuts disclosure down.

items.fail: “It’s only slightly raised — we’ll repeat it in three months.”
items.why: Macrocytosis is a finding to explain. Rechecking without a work-up misses B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease and the alcohol.
items.fix: Arrange B12, folate, TSH, liver tests, reticulocytes and a film, and take an alcohol history.

items.fail: Listing leukaemia among possible causes to be thorough.
items.why: She rang frightened of exactly that. Unbalanced lists increase anxiety and reduce trust.
items.fix: Reassure honestly first: “With the rest of your count normal, this is very rarely leukaemia.”

items.fail: Asking “Do you drink too much?” and accepting “no, not really”.
items.why: A loaded question invites denial and misses the most likely cause and the grief behind it.
items.fix: Normalise: “Alcohol is a common cause, so I ask everyone — no judgement.” Then pause and let her answer.

items.fail: Advising her to stop drinking completely from tonight.
items.why: If she is dependent, abrupt cessation risks withdrawal. NICE CG100 covers assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: Screen for morning shakes and sweats; agree a gradual goal; “If you get shaky when cutting down, ring us — don’t stop suddenly.”

items.fail: Treating the drinking without asking about mood or suicide risk.
items.why: Grief, low mood and alcohol together raise risk; missing this is a serious omission.
items.fix: “How have you been in yourself?” then ask directly about thoughts of self-harm.

items.fail: Ending the phone call without confirming the plan or a follow-up.
items.why: Telephone consultations need explicit checks; no follow-up is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back, a results call, and a review in about four weeks.
